intro: The law on what counts as evidence in court and how facts are proved. In force since 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. It gives electronic and digital records the same standing as paper documents.

sections.p: 'Document' includes electronic and digital records — emails, server logs, files on computers and phones, messages, websites, location data and voice mail. Oral evidence includes statements given electronically.
Whoever wants the court to rule in their favour based on a fact must prove that fact. In criminal cases, the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
A confession obtained by inducement, threat, coercion or promise from a person in authority is not admissible in a criminal case.

A confession made to a police officer cannot be used against the accused. A confession made in police custody is also inadmissible unless made in the immediate presence of a magistrate. Exception: if information from the accused leads to the discovery of a fact (e.g. a weapon), that part can be proved.

A statement by a person about the cause of their death or the circumstances leading to it is admissible, even though they can't be cross-examined. Courts may convict on it alone if it's found truthful and voluntary.
Opinions of experts in science, art, handwriting, fingerprints, and now explicitly 'any other field', are relevant — including examiners of electronic evidence.

The document itself is primary evidence. For electronic records, each copy stored in multiple places, or created and stored simultaneously, counts as primary evidence, as do records produced from proper custody.
Nothing in the Adhiniyam can deny the admissibility of an electronic or digital record merely because it's electronic — it has the same legal effect as a paper document.

To use an electronic record as evidence, a certificate in the prescribed format (in the Schedule) must be submitted, signed by the person in charge of the device and by an expert. It covers how the record was produced and that the device was working properly.

sections.t: Abetment of suicide of a married woman
sections.p: If a woman dies by suicide within 7 years of marriage and was subjected to cruelty by her husband or his relatives, the court may presume they abetted it.
If it's shown a woman was subjected to cruelty or harassment for dowry soon before her death, the court shall presume the person responsible caused the dowry death.

sections.t: Absence of consent in rape cases
sections.p: In certain rape prosecutions, where intercourse is proved and the woman states in court that she did not consent, the court shall presume she did not consent.
Everyone is competent to testify unless the court finds they can't understand questions or give rational answers due to young age, old age, illness or similar reasons.
A spouse can't be compelled to disclose communications made by the other during marriage, except in cases between the spouses or where one is prosecuted for a crime against the other.
A lawyer can't disclose communications with a client made in the course of professional engagement, unless the client consents or the communication was to further an illegal purpose.
